body.objective: Students will be able to develop a concept.
successCriteria: I can develop a clear concept from an issue or question
I can choose media and form that strengthen the concept
I can document how my concept developed
body.hook: When Rebecca Belmore set up a giant wooden megaphone in a meadow in 1991 and invited people to speak to the land, the "artwork" wasn't the megaphone. It was the idea, and the voices. Contemporary artists often start with a concept and choose whatever media best carries it.

vocabulary.definition: The central idea or message an artwork communicates.
Art in which the idea is more important than traditional skill or beauty.
An artwork that transforms a space the viewer enters or moves through.
Art made for one particular place.
A short text explaining the concept and choices in an artwork.

study.title: Idea First
study.question: How do artists turn an idea into the right form?
study.passage:
Part 1, Starting points (10 minutes): Write three issues or questions that matter to you (for example waste, belonging, memory, screens, climate, language).
Part 2, Concept statement (10 minutes): For one, write a one-sentence concept: "My work explores ___ by ___ so that viewers ___."
Part 3, Form matching (15 minutes): Brainstorm five possible forms for the same concept: painting, sculpture, installation, video or digital work, performance, photo series, textile. For each, note what it adds or loses.
Part 4, Artist research (10 minutes): Look at one contemporary artist whose form fits your idea: Rebecca Belmore (performance and installation), Brian Jungen (sculpture from Nike shoes reshaped as masks), Ai Weiwei (installation), or Shary Boyle (sculpture and projection).
Part 5, Proposal (15 minutes): Sketch the chosen form with notes on materials, scale, site and how the viewer will experience it.
study.source: Original studio task written for this lesson; artist examples summarized from public gallery sources.
steps: List issues that matter to you
Match the concept to five possible forms
discussion: Why might an installation communicate an idea better than a painting?
How does Brian Jungen's choice of material add meaning?
Can a concept be strong but the execution weak?
How will viewers know what your concept is?
study.product: Submit a concept proposal: concept sentence, form comparison, annotated sketch, materials list and a draft artist statement of 100 words.

examples.title: Concept sentence
examples.problem: Write a concept sentence about waste.
examples.answer: My work explores everyday waste by building a sculpture from one week of my family's packaging so that viewers see their own habits

examples.title: Material meaning
examples.problem: Why did Brian Jungen use Nike sneakers?
examples.answer: Reshaping mass-produced shoes into Northwest Coast-style masks comments on consumerism and cultural identity
examples.explore: How does the material change the meaning?

examples.title: Site-specific
examples.problem: How could a site change a work about silence?
examples.answer: Installing it in a busy hallway makes silence feel stronger by contrast

examples.title: Form choice
examples.problem: Compare painting vs installation for a work on isolation.
examples.answer: An installation could place the viewer alone in a small space, making them feel isolation

practice.a: The central idea an artwork communicates.
An artwork that transforms a space the viewer enters.

practice.q: Complete: My work explores ___ by ___ so that viewers ___.
Why compare several forms for one concept?
practice.a: To find the form that best communicates the idea.
What a material is and where it comes from adds associations.
Art where the idea is more important than traditional skill or beauty.

practice.q: Name a contemporary Canadian artist and their medium.
practice.a: Rebecca Belmore, performance and installation (other valid answers).

practice.q: What should a proposal sketch include?
practice.a: Materials, scale, site and viewer experience.

practice.q: Can conceptual art still require skill? Explain.
practice.a: Yes; skill in planning, choosing and presenting form.

practice.q: How does viewer experience differ between a painting and an installation?
practice.a: Viewers look at a painting; they enter and move through an installation.

practice.q: Why might an artist choose temporary art?
practice.a: To make a point about time, change or place, or to avoid permanence.

practice.q: How can an artist make sure the concept is understood?
practice.a: Clear form choices, titles and an artist statement.

misconceptions: Thinking conceptual art requires no effort
Choosing a medium before an idea
Thinking an artist statement can replace a weak artwork
exitTicket: Name the form you chose and one reason.
